sources.title: Michael Witzel: Early Sanskritization, Origins and Development of the Kuru State
sources.note: Specialist Vedic synthesis used for the overview and map-cutoff summary: Kuru and Panchala were close but separately led peoples linked through ritual rivalry, learning and elite marriage.

sources.title: INFLIBNET: Mahajanapadas, Rise of Magadha, Nandas and the Invasion of Alexander
sources.note: University teaching chapter used for textual-source disagreement, janapada formation, the sixteen-state list, settlement growth, agriculture, NBPW and punch-marked coins.

sources.title: Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.45: Uposatha Sutta
sources.note: Primary Pali transmission used for the formula naming Kuru and Pañcāla separately among sixteen countries; the canon is not treated as a fifth-century inscription.

sources.title: B. C. Law: Pañchālas and Their Capital Ahichchhatra
sources.note: Archaeological Survey of India memoir used cautiously for literary geography, northern and southern divisions, Ahichchhatra, Kampilya and the limits of political reconstruction.

sources.title: A. K. Pokharia et al.: Botanical Findings from Excavations at Ahichchhatra
sources.note: Peer-reviewed archaeobotanical study used for site identity, stratigraphy, crop remains, seasonality and explicit dating and preservation limits.

sources.title: Archaeological Survey of India: The Pottery of Ahichchhatra
sources.note: Excavation report used for Painted Grey Ware, Northern Black Polished Ware, vessel forms and the uncertainty of older ceramic chronologies.

sources.title: Archaeological Survey of India: Indian Archaeology 1964 to 1965, A Review
sources.note: Official fieldwork review used for the Ahichchhatra sequence from ochre-coloured pottery through PGW, NBPW and later periods.

sources.title: Archaeological Survey of India: Archaeology and Tradition
sources.note: Official archaeological study used to distinguish material evidence from later epic tradition and to place northern and southern Panchala PGW sites.

sources.title: Ground-penetrating radar at the ancient capitals of Panchala and Vatsa
sources.note: Peer-reviewed geophysical study used for Ahichchhatra’s identification, buried walls and residential anomalies, with the warning that deep features span a long occupation.

sources.title: UNESCO History of Civilizations of Central Asia I: The Painted Grey Ware Culture of the Iron Age
sources.note: Scholarly regional synthesis used for wattle-and-daub houses, hearths, iron objects and cautiously interpreted toys and game pieces.

sources.title: INFLIBNET: Iron Age, Antiquity of Iron in India
sources.note: University archaeology chapter used for PGW distribution, dates, iron-working evidence and the warning that an artifact style is not a named kingdom.

sources.title: University of Pennsylvania Museum: The Ganga-Yamuna Basin
sources.note: Museum archaeological synthesis used for rivers, settlement size, early-house uncertainty, the PGW to NBPW transition and the later emergence of writing and coinage.

sources.title: GRETIL: Chāndogya Upaniṣad, Sanskrit text
sources.note: Scholarly electronic Sanskrit text used for the original Vedic Sanskrit sentence naming the assembly of the Panchalas.

sources.title: Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.3.1: Sanskrit, transliteration and translation
sources.note: Text-and-translation page used to check transliteration, translation and the Śvetaketu to Pravāhaṇa teaching scene.

sources.title: UNESCO Intangible Heritage: Tradition of Vedic Chanting
sources.note: UNESCO description used only to explain the exacting oral transmission techniques behind Vedic texts, not to reconstruct a universal Panchala school.

sources.title: INFLIBNET: Vedic Culture
sources.note: University overview used as broad literary context for social ranks, patriarchal households, food and clothing, always distinguished from direct fifth-century Panchala observation.

sources.title: IGNOU: The Early Vedic Society
sources.note: University history unit used as broad comparative evidence for kin-based households, patriarchy, women’s visibility and oral learning; it is not treated as a fifth-century census.

sources.title: Atharva-Veda Saṃhitā IV.12: Charm to Cure Serious Wounds
sources.note: Primary Vedic healing hymn used as evidence for ritual healing ideas about joining bone, marrow, flesh and skin, not as proof of clinical effectiveness or a Panchala hospital.

sources.title: Archaeological Survey of India: Ancient India 10 to 11, Excavations at Hastināpura
sources.note: Regional excavation report used for later NBPW drains, soakage jars and ring wells at neighboring Hastinapura, explicitly not relabelled as Panchala toilets.

sources.title: British Museum: Coin of the Pancala kingdom, Bhanumitra
sources.note: Museum collection record used for a much later copper Panchala coin, its ruler attribution and broad 150 BCE to 300 CE date range.

sources.title: National Mission on Monuments and Antiquities: Bhanumitra coin from Ahichchhatra
sources.note: Indian national antiquities record used for provenance, copper medium, Panchala symbols and the Brahmi ruler legend.

proposedOverrides.summary: The 400 BCE endpoint is only the atlas coverage seam; no conquest or extinction is known there.

batchIdentityNotes: The exact imported id is pancala, displayed Pancala and indexed circa 500 to 400 BCE; historical discussion explains Panchala and Pañcāla without changing the id.
Initial coverage records one 500 to 400 border interval, one border file, an imported summary and no card or override.
The exact feature is absent at 700 BCE, present once at 500 BCE, absent at the indexed 400 BCE endpoint and absent at 300 BCE.
The 500 BCE target is one Polygon with one part, one ring and fifteen positions; bounds are [78.88938889388896,25.81163945055725,82.34542345423455,28.93603224081083].
The raw coordinate SHA-256 is b49ac36f9ee5cba36451719a5e669096056efce04315d81daec420f10e9e5e75; the canonical hash is 70735000695a712e8170821acbbed5c19d700c6b60a2da4de2591498e1025c1e.
The polygon contains Kampilya, Kannauj, Farrukhabad, Shravasti and Ayodhya, but excludes Ahichchhatra, Bareilly and Budaun; this is a major historical-geography mismatch.
Kuru, Kosala, Kasi, Vatsa, Surasena, Malla, Magadha, Avanti, Gandhara and the broad Hindu kingdoms layer remain separate exact atlas identities.
Every geometry statement describes imported display data only; no coordinate proves ethnicity, language, ancient survey boundaries or exclusive sovereignty.
